issues.issue: The minimum interest charge deems the average Daily Balance to have been $20,000,000, and Section 2.10(c) separately charges an unused line fee computed on the excess of the Maximum Revolver Amount over the greater of the actual average balance "or $20,000,000 during the Minimum Interest Period". Whether the two provisions together charge twice for the same undrawn $20,000,000 is not resolved by either.

The capital-adequacy charge is triggered by a reduction in return "by any amount deemed by Lender to be material", calculated by Lender using "any reasonable averaging and attribution methods", and the resulting statement is "deemed true and correct absent manifest error". None of those standards is defined, so the amount payable rests on the Lender's own determination.

This subsection offers the option only to have interest "on all of the Advances" determined by the LIBOR Rate, while Section 2.12(b) speaks of an election "for a permitted portion of the Advances". Whether the Borrowers may split the loan between Base Rate and LIBOR tranches cannot be answered without choosing between the two subsections.

The notice provision contemplates an election "for a permitted portion of the Advances and an Interest Period", but Section 2.12(a) and the deemed-election rule in Section 2.12(c) both operate on an all-or-nothing basis covering "all of the Advances", and nothing in the agreement says what portions are "permitted". The two subsections cannot both be given effect.

This subsection deems the LIBOR Option elected for every Interest Period unless the Borrower opts out, whereas Section 2.12(a) provides that at the end of an Interest Period a LIBOR Rate Loan "automatically shall convert" to the Base Rate "unless Administrative Borrower properly has exercised the LIBOR Option". The default setting is opposite in the two subsections.

Lender may terminate the LIBOR Option whenever, "in the reasonable opinion of Lender", any change in market conditions makes it "unlawful or impractical" to fund or maintain LIBOR Rate Loans — "impractical" and "change in market conditions" being nowhere defined, and Section 2.12(e) confirming that Lender need not match-fund at all. What circumstances suffice is left to the Lender's opinion.

The subsection makes each Borrower's obligations absolute "irrespective of the validity, regularity or enforceability of this Agreement or any other circumstances whatsoever", which purports to survive the unenforceability of the very instrument creating the obligation. It also cross-refers to "this Section 2.15", a section that does not exist in the agreement.

The waiver is framed entirely in terms of "Section 580(d) of the California Code of Civil Procedure", yet Section 13(a) provides that construction, interpretation and enforcement of this Agreement are "GOVERNED BY ... THE LAWS OF THE STATE OF NEW YORK". Whether a New York-governed contract can waive California antideficiency protections, and what the clause means if California law does not apply, cannot be settled without reading the two together.

This waiver of "all rights and defenses that such Borrower may have because the Obligations are secured by Real Property" presupposes the California one-action and antideficiency regime, while Section 13(a) makes New York law govern the Agreement. The clause's operative content depends on which state's law supplies the rights being waived.

Clause (B) provides that "Agent and Lenders may collect from such Borrower", but this is a bilateral agreement with a single "Lender" and no "Agent" — neither term is defined here. Who holds the right the clause confers, and whether it operates at all, is a defect in the clause's own words.

The condition requires Lender to have completed a sprawling list of diligence items "the results of which shall be satisfactory to Lender", with no standard of reasonableness and no deemed-satisfaction mechanism. Read with the preamble's statement that funding is "conclusively deemed" satisfaction or waiver, whether the condition ever had content is contestable.

Reference checks on four named individuals must produce results "satisfactory to Lender in its sole discretion", a standard that appears nowhere else among the Section 3.1 conditions, which use "satisfactory to Lender" simpliciter. Whether "sole discretion" displaces the good-faith limits implied elsewhere is a question on the face of the clause.

The condition demands that Borrowers actually hold all required licenses and be "in compliance with any applicable federal or state statutes or regulations regarding Fund's offering, sale or redemption of the Investor Membership Interests", and then dissolves that demand with a proviso that it "may be satisfied by Fund providing to Lender such reasonable assurances as Lender may require". A promise of assurances is not compliance, and the two halves of the clause pull apart.

The eight documents listed here for the initial $250,000,000 of pledged notes do not match the nine-item list in clause (r) of the "Eligible Notes Receivable" definition, which additionally requires evidence of casualty insurance and a recorded collateral assignment. Because Section 3.3(e) and Section 8.17 both police the $250,000,000 pool by reference to "the documents required by Section 3.1(t)", the discrepancy between the two lists is operative.

After twenty enumerated conditions the section closes with "all other documents and legal matters in connection with the transactions contemplated by this Agreement shall have been delivered, executed, or recorded and shall be in form and substance satisfactory to Lender". Whether that catch-all is limited by the specific conditions preceding it, or is a free-standing condition of unlimited scope, is a general-versus-specific problem in the clause itself.

The preamble to Section 3.2 states that failure to satisfy a condition subsequent itself constitutes an Event of Default, while Section 8.2(c) treats "failure to satisfy a condition subsequent set forth in Section 3.2 within the period stated" as a default only if it "continues for a period of 20 Business Days". Whether the Controller-hiring failure defaults the loan at once or after a cure period cannot be answered from either provision alone.

The condition that "no Material Adverse Change shall have occurred" fixes no baseline date against which the change is measured, and the defined term itself reaches "prospects" without further limit. Because this is a condition to every Advance, the absence of a measurement point governs whether Lender may stop funding.

The termination sentence is internally contradictory: it makes Lender's right to terminate "subject to any notice and cure rights otherwise provided by this Agreement" and in the same breath permits termination "immediately and without notice" upon an Event of Default. Whether the cure periods in Section 8.2 must run before termination is left unresolved by the clause's own words.

The clause imposes the prepayment premium as agreed liquidated damages on terminations including "termination upon the election of Lender ... after the occurrence and during the continuation of an Event of Default" and confirmation of a plan of reorganization, but then qualifies the obligation with the undefined words "if applicable". Whether the premium is owed in a bankruptcy plan context, and what "if applicable" refers to, is left open.

This section requires original notes "sufficient to ensure that Lender ... at all times holds Eligible Notes Receivable having an aggregate outstanding principal amount of not less than $250,000,000", yet Section 4.9(a) obliges Lender to return each note on repayment and Section 4.9(b) on sale, which can drop the pool below the floor without any act of the Borrower. How the two are reconciled — and whether Section 8.17's three-day cure is the answer — is not stated here.

Clauses (b), (e) and (f) of the power of attorney are expressly limited to times when an Event of Default has occurred and is continuing, while clauses (c) and (d) — verification inquiries to Account Debtors and endorsement of the Borrower's payment items — carry no such limitation. The enumeration invites an expressio unius reading that Lender may exercise those powers at any time, including before default.

This section lets Lender direct liquidation of Deposit and Securities Accounts "[u]pon the occurrence and during the continuance of a Default or Event of Default", whereas Section 9.1 makes every other remedy available only "[u]pon the occurrence, and during the continuation, of an Event of Default". Whether Lender may seize account balances on a mere Default — an event that by definition has not yet ripened — is a conflict between the two provisions.

Servicing rights may be revoked only "after the occurrence and during the continuation of an Event of Default" and then "by giving notice to Administrative Borrower in accordance with the terms of the Servicing Agreement", while Section 9.1(e) lets Lender "terminate the Servicing Agreement and assign servicing responsibilities to any replacement servicer". Whether the procedures of the Servicing Agreement bind Lender when it acts under Section 9.1 is not resolved here.

The subsection requires Lender to return a repaid note "to Administrative Borrower to facilitate its payment" and to release its Lien "promptly upon receipt of the final payment", although the note is described as already "repaid in its entirety". The sequence — repaid, then returned to facilitate payment, then released on final payment — is internally inconsistent.

Clause (c) warrants that each identified note "is not excluded as ineligible by virtue of one or more of the excluding criteria set forth in the definition of Eligible Notes Receivable", while that definition in turn defines Eligible Notes Receivable as notes "that comply with each of the representations and warranties respecting Eligible Notes Receivable made in the Loan Documents". The two provisions define each other in a circle.

The sentence that "[a]ny Offering Circular ... all Investor Membership Interests issued by Fund, and all aspects of Borrowers' operations, comply with all applicable federal, state and local laws and regulations" is stated without the materiality qualifier that governs the sentences around it and without any knowledge limitation. How absolute a securities-law compliance warranty this creates is a question on its own words.

The representation carves out anything "described on Schedule 5.8 or in an Offering Circular", and "Offering Circular" is defined to include the private offering memorandum "as amended from time to time" together with all subscription agreements. The exception can therefore expand after closing without Lender's assent, so what the Borrower has actually warranted about its capital Stock is indeterminate.

The disclosure warranty is qualified three times by the phrase "(taken as a whole)", which is nowhere defined and leaves it unclear whether a single false statement can breach the representation or only a misleading overall picture. Section 8.11 makes "any material misstatement or misrepresentation" an Event of Default, so the aggregation qualifier is doing real work.

The representation that no listed title company "is an Affiliate of Borrower" must be tested under the definition of "Affiliate", whose expanded 10%-ownership, director and joint-venture rules apply only "for purposes of the definition of Eligible Notes Receivable and Section 7.13 hereof". Which version of "Affiliate" governs this representation is unresolved between the two provisions.

The reporting schedule ends with the open-ended item "(h) such other reports as to the Collateral or the financial condition of each Borrower and its Subsidiaries, as Lender may request", following seven specifically described reports with fixed deadlines. Whether that catch-all is bounded by the enumerated categories — and what deadline attaches to it, given that breach of Section 6.2 is an immediate Event of Default under Section 8.2(a) — is left open.
